questions.stem: Sedimentary rocks can form with clastic, chemical, or biochemical textures. Describe the difference between a clastic texture and a biochemical texture, and give one example rock for each.
questions.sample_answer: Clastic texture is made of broken fragments (clasts) of pre-existing rocks or minerals that have been weathered, eroded, transported, and then compacted/cemented together (e.g., sandstone, shale, or conglomerate). Biochemical texture forms from the accumulation of organic or skeletal material, such as shell fragments or plant matter, that becomes compacted and cemented into rock (e.g., coal, fossil limestone, or coquina). Accept other valid examples from the Rocks and Minerals List.

questions.stem: Image 5 is a diagram of Bowen's Reaction Series. Using the diagram, explain why a rock rich in olivine (such as peridotite) tends to weather and break down more quickly at Earth's surface than a rock rich in quartz.
questions.sample_answer: Olivine crystallizes from magma at the highest temperatures on Bowen's Reaction Series, which are the farthest from Earth's surface temperature and pressure conditions, making olivine the least chemically stable at the surface and therefore the quickest to weather. Quartz crystallizes last, at the lowest temperature on the series, closest to surface conditions, which makes it the most chemically stable and most resistant to weathering.

answer_spec.rubric: Pack gives a sample answer only; no point-by-point rubric. Needs a human-written rubric before auto/AI grading.

questions.note: Key relies on the weathering-stability corollary of Bowen's series (Goldich); the diagram shows crystallization order only. Correct and commonly tested.

questions.stem: Describe one complete pathway through the rock cycle by which a sedimentary rock could eventually become a metamorphic rock. Name the geologic process(es) involved at each step.
questions.sample_answer: Example pathway: Weathering and erosion break down existing rock into sediment; the sediment is transported and deposited in a new environment; burial, compaction, and cementation lithify the sediment into a sedimentary rock (e.g., shale); continued burial and tectonic activity then expose the rock to heat and/or pressure, causing recrystallization and deformation (metamorphism) that produces a metamorphic rock (e.g., slate). Accept other valid, logically ordered pathways and rock examples.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between cleavage and fracture as diagnostic properties of minerals, and give one example mineral for each.
questions.sample_answer: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along smooth, flat planes related to planes of weakness in its crystal structure (e.g., mica, which cleaves into thin sheets). Fracture is the tendency of a mineral to break along irregular, non-planar surfaces because it lacks such planes of weakness (e.g., quartz, which shows conchoidal fracture).

questions.stem: A shale layer is buried and changes into slate. Much later, the slate is uplifted, exposed, and broken into sediment. Identify the two major rock-cycle transformations and the processes responsible for each.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a clastic sedimentary texture and a biochemical sedimentary texture, and give one example rock for each.
questions.sample_answer: Clastic texture is made of broken fragments (clasts) of pre-existing rocks or minerals that have been weathered, eroded, transported, and then compacted/cemented together (e.g., sandstone, shale, or conglomerate). Biochemical texture forms from the accumulation of organic or skeletal material, such as shell fragments or plant matter, that becomes compacted and cemented into rock (e.g., coal, fossil limestone, or coquina). questions.stem: Using Bowen's Reaction Series (Image 8), explain why a rock rich in olivine tends to weather more quickly at Earth's surface than a rock rich in quartz.
questions.sample_answer: Olivine crystallizes from magma at the highest temperatures on Bowen's Reaction Series, which are the farthest from Earth's surface temperature and pressure conditions, making olivine the least chemically stable at the surface and therefore the quickest to weather. Quartz crystallizes last, at the lowest temperature on the series, closest to surface conditions, which makes it the most chemically stable and most resistant to weathering.

questions.stem: Describe the difference between regional and contact metamorphism, including a typical geologic setting for each.
questions.sample_answer: Regional metamorphism affects large areas of rock and is caused by the high heat and pressure typically associated with mountain-building (tectonic plate collision) over a broad region. Contact metamorphism is localized and occurs when rock is altered by heat from a nearby igneous intrusion, such as where magma comes into contact with surrounding country rock, typically affecting only a narrow zone around the intrusion.

questions.stem: A student is given a mineral specimen with rhombohedral cleavage in three directions, none of which are at right angles, and the specimen reacts vigorously with dilute HCl. Identify the most likely mineral, and explain which TWO diagnostic properties were used to identify it.
questions.sample_answer: The mineral is most likely calcite. The two diagnostic properties used are: (1) rhombohedral cleavage in three directions not at 90 degrees, characteristic of calcite's crystal structure, and (2) a strong/vigorous reaction (effervescence) with dilute HCl, which calcite exhibits readily (unlike dolomite, which reacts slowly or only when powdered).

questions.stem: Explain why streak is generally considered a more reliable diagnostic property than a minerals exterior color.
questions.sample_answer: A mineral's exterior color can be affected by weathering, surface impurities, or slight variations in trace element content, and can vary widely even within the same mineral species. Streak, the color of a mineral's powder, is more consistent because it reflects the true color of the mineral with fewer surface effects, making it a more reliable diagnostic property. Rhodochrosite, for example, is often a distinctive pink but leaves a white streak.

questions.stem: Quartz is used both in glassmaking and in electronic timing devices. Explain one property of quartz that supports each use.
questions.sample_answer: Quartz is a common, chemically stable source of silica, so high-purity quartz can be melted to manufacture glass. Quartz is also piezoelectric: mechanical stress produces an electrical response, and a quartz crystal oscillates at a stable frequency in clocks and electronic timing devices.

questions.stem: Explain the relationship between grain size and the energy of the environment of deposition, using two specific examples of environments and their typical grain sizes.
questions.sample_answer: Higher-energy environments, where water or wind moves quickly, can carry and deposit larger, coarser sediment particles (e.g., an alluvial fan or a beach, which typically has coarse sand, gravel, or pebbles). Lower-energy environments, where water movement is slow or still, can only carry and deposit very fine particles (e.g., a lake/lacustrine or deep marine environment, which typically accumulates fine silt and clay).

questions.stem: Explain the difference between an intrusive and an extrusive igneous environment, and describe one landform or rock body associated with each.
questions.sample_answer: Intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks form when magma cools and solidifies below Earth's surface, generally cooling slowly and producing larger crystals (phaneritic texture); an example landform is a batholith, a large body of intrusive igneous rock. Extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks form when magma (lava) erupts and cools at Earth's surface, generally cooling quickly and producing fine-grained or glassy textures; an example is a lava flow.

questions.stem: Explain how fractional crystallization, as illustrated by Bowen's Reaction Series (Image 8), can produce a range of igneous rock compositions from a single parent magma.
questions.sample_answer: As magma cools, minerals crystallize in the predictable sequence described by Bowen's Reaction Series. If early-formed crystals (such as olivine) are removed from the melt, for example by settling out of the magma chamber, before they can continue reacting with the remaining liquid, the composition of the remaining magma shifts away from that of the removed crystals, typically becoming more silica-rich over time. Repeating this crystal-removal process at each stage of the series can generate a whole sequence of different igneous rock compositions, from mafic to felsic, starting from a single parent magma.

questions.stem: Explain the relationship between a mineral's crystal system and its physical properties, using TWO example minerals in your answer.
questions.sample_answer: A mineral's crystal system describes the symmetry and axial relationships of its internal atomic structure, which in turn controls external physical properties such as crystal shape and cleavage direction. For example, minerals in the cubic system, such as garnet or pyrite, tend to have highly symmetric crystal forms (cubes, dodecahedra); pyrite commonly forms cubic crystals as a direct expression of its cubic crystal system. Spodumene, by contrast, crystallizes in the monoclinic system, which has lower symmetry, and correspondingly forms elongated, flattened prismatic crystals with two directions of cleavage at nearly 90°, reflecting its less symmetric internal structure.

questions.stem: Explain why accurate identification of rocks and minerals generally relies on multiple diagnostic properties rather than a single property, using an example of a case where relying on color alone could lead to a misidentification.
questions.sample_answer: A single property, especially color, can be shared by many different minerals or can vary within a single mineral species due to trace element impurities, weathering, or surface staining, so it is rarely diagnostic by itself. Using multiple independent properties together (e.g., hardness, streak, cleavage, luster, and reaction to acid) narrows down the possibilities far more reliably. For example, both pyrite and gold can appear brassy yellow in color, but they can be readily distinguished using other properties: pyrite is much harder, has a greenish-black to black streak, and is brittle, while gold is very soft, has a golden-yellow streak, and is malleable rather than brittle.

questions.stem: Explain what a mineral group is, and describe how members of the same mineral group can share important physical properties while still differing from one another. Use the mica group as your example.
questions.sample_answer: A mineral group is a set of minerals that share a similar crystal structure and related, though not identical, chemical compositions. Because members of a group share the same underlying structure, they often share key physical properties; for example, all members of the mica group (such as biotite and muscovite) share excellent one-direction (basal) cleavage because of their common sheet-silicate structure. However, individual members can still differ in other properties, such as color, due to differences in exact chemical composition — biotite is dark-colored due to its iron and magnesium content, while muscovite is typically colorless to light-colored because it lacks these elements.

questions.stem: Image 10 is a diagram of Bowen's Reaction Series. Describe Bowen's Reaction Series in detail, including both the discontinuous and continuous branches. Explain what the series tells us about (a) the order in which minerals crystallize from a cooling, mafic magma, and (b) why rocks rich in early-crystallizing minerals (such as olivine) tend to weather more quickly at Earth's surface than rocks rich in late-crystallizing minerals (such as quartz).
questions.sample_answer: Bowen's Reaction Series describes the predictable order in which silicate minerals crystallize from a cooling, mafic magma. It has two branches occurring simultaneously: a discontinuous branch, in which distinct mineral species crystallize in sequence as temperature drops — olivine, then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite mica — with each mineral reacting with the remaining melt to form the next; and a continuous branch, in which plagioclase feldspar continuously changes composition from calcium-rich to sodium-rich as temperature drops, without changing to a different mineral species. The two branches converge at lower temperatures, where potassium feldspar, then muscovite mica, then quartz crystallize last. (a) This order tells us that minerals like olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase crystallize first, at the highest temperatures, while quartz crystallizes last, at the lowest temperature, closest to Earth's surface conditions. (b) Minerals that crystallize at high temperature, far from Earth's surface conditions, are the least chemically stable when exposed to surface weathering, so olivine-rich rocks weather and break down relatively quickly. Quartz, crystallizing last at conditions closest to the surface, is the most chemically stable and therefore the most resistant to weathering — part of why quartz is so common in sediment and sedimentary rocks such as sandstone.

questions.stem: Describe the complete rock cycle, explaining how each of the three main rock types (igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic) can be transformed into each of the other two types, as well as into a new rock of the same type. Name at least one specific geologic process responsible for each transformation you describe.
questions.sample_answer: Igneous rock can become sedimentary rock through weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, and lithification (compaction and cementation) of the resulting sediment. Igneous rock can become metamorphic rock through burial and exposure to heat and/or pressure, causing recrystallization and deformation without melting. Igneous rock can become new igneous rock if it is melted and recrystallizes. Sedimentary rock can become metamorphic rock through the same heat/pressure recrystallization process. Sedimentary rock can become igneous rock if it is buried deeply enough to melt and then cools and crystallizes. Sedimentary rock can become new sedimentary rock if it is weathered, eroded, and re-deposited. Metamorphic rock can become igneous rock if it is melted and recrystallizes. Metamorphic rock can become sedimentary rock through uplift, weathering, erosion, and lithification. Metamorphic rock can become new (often higher-grade) metamorphic rock if it is subjected to additional heat and/or pressure. In all cases, the underlying processes are: melting and crystallization; weathering, erosion, and deposition; compaction and cementation; and heat/pressure-driven recrystallization and deformation.

questions.stem: Explain the concept of an index mineral and how geologists use a sequence of index minerals to determine the grade (intensity) of regional metamorphism that a rock has experienced. Describe the general progression of index minerals from low to high metamorphic grade, and explain why a single parent rock (such as shale), subjected to regional metamorphism across a mountain belt, might show different index minerals in different locations.
questions.sample_answer: An index mineral is a mineral that forms only within a specific, relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure conditions during metamorphism, so its presence in a rock indicates the approximate grade (intensity) of metamorphism that rock experienced. As shale undergoes progressively more intense regional metamorphism, it typically develops index minerals in roughly the following order from low to high grade: chlorite, then biotite, then garnet, then staurolite, then kyanite, then sillimanite. Because the intensity of heat and pressure during a regional metamorphic event is usually not uniform across an entire mountain belt — it is generally more intense closer to the zone of most direct tectonic collision or deepest burial, and less intense farther away — the same original parent rock (shale) can end up at different metamorphic grades in different locations, developing different index minerals (for example, chlorite near the edge of the metamorphosed zone and sillimanite near its most intensely metamorphosed core).

questions.stem: Using your knowledge of igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic processes, explain how a single episode of mountain-building (regional tectonic collision) could produce examples of all three main rock types within the same general area. Describe one plausible, specific rock example of each type that could form as a result.
questions.sample_answer: During a regional tectonic collision, crustal rocks are thickened, buried, and subjected to intense heat and pressure, causing deeply buried rocks to undergo regional metamorphism into metamorphic rocks — for example, shale being transformed into schist. In some cases, especially deep burial and heat can cause partial melting of crustal material; this magma can then cool and crystallize underground, forming intrusive igneous rock, such as granite, or reach the surface and erupt, forming extrusive igneous rock. At the same time, the collision uplifts rock to Earth's surface, where it is exposed to weathering and erosion; the resulting sediment is transported into nearby basins and deposited, where burial, compaction, and cementation lithify it into sedimentary rock, such as sandstone or shale. In this way, a single mountain-building event can simultaneously produce metamorphic rock (e.g., schist) at depth, igneous rock (e.g., granite) from partial melting, and sedimentary rock (e.g., sandstone) in adjacent basins from eroded material.
